caseNote: 가상 사례 (식료품 체인 사내 분석팀, 건물 수리 업체) + 실제 연구·저술 (Morgan & Hunt 1994, Maister·Green·Galford 2000)
insight: 기업 고객은 오늘의 제품이 아니라 문제가 생겼을 때 당신이 어떻게 행동할지를 산다. 신뢰는 감정이 아니라 지켜진 약속의 기록이다.
misconception: 더 좋은 제품이나 더 싼 가격이면 이긴다. 관계란 식사와 선물로 쌓는 친분이다.

sources.text: Morgan, R. M., & Hunt, S. D. (1994). The Commitment-Trust Theory of Relationship Marketing. Journal of Marketing, 58(3), 20–38.
Maister, D. H., Green, C. H., & Galford, R. M. (2000). The Trusted Advisor. Free Press.
식료품 체인과 건물 수리 업체 사례, 30% 비용 증가는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Morgan & Hunt(1994)의 핵심 주장(신뢰와 몰입이 관계 마케팅의 중심 변수)을 카드 4에서 일반적으로 요약했습니다. 서지 정보(권·호·쪽)를 게시 전 원문으로 확인하세요.
The Trusted Advisor의 신뢰 공식은 (Credibility + Reliability + Intimacy) ÷ Self-orientation입니다. 카드 5에서 Intimacy를 'closeness'로 쉽게 풀어 썼습니다. 표현이 원뜻을 해치지 않는지 확인하세요.
식료품 체인(매장 40곳), 6개월, 수리 비용 30% 증가는 모두 가상 수치입니다. 실제 통계처럼 읽히지 않도록 해당 카드에 illustrative 표시를 붙였습니다.

cards.title: The better tool nobody wanted
body: The analytics team at a grocery chain built a new ordering forecast for its 40 stores. In tests, it cut wasted produce. It was free to every store.
Six months later, most store managers still ordered from their own spreadsheets. The tool wasn't the problem.

image.label: A shiny new dashboard ignored next to a worn spreadsheet
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 마트 사무실 책상 위에 반짝이는 새 대시보드 화면은 먼지가 앉아 있고, 옆의 낡고 커피 얼룩 묻은 종이 스프레드시트를 매장 관리자가 들여다보는 장면. 실제 마트 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You lead that analytics team.
body: Store managers say the tool "looks fine". Off the record, they bring up last year: your team's sales report broke during the holiday rush, and two promised fixes arrived months late.

options.text: Ask the operations VP to make the tool mandatory
options.feedback: You get logins, not belief. Managers can open the tool and still order from their spreadsheets, and now they trust your team even less.

options.text: Run a big demo showing how accurate the forecasts are
options.feedback: Proof helps your credibility. But the doubt isn't about accuracy. It's about whether your team shows up when something breaks.

options.text: Start with three stores, promise a fix within a week for anything that breaks, and keep that promise
options.feedback: Slower, but it rebuilds what managers are really judging: your team's record. Kept promises travel between stores by word of mouth.

cards.title: They weren't judging the tool. They were judging the team.
body: A store manager who orders wrong carries the cost: empty shelves or rotting stock. Switching to the forecast meant depending on the analytics team every week, in situations nobody could predict.
The managers had one piece of evidence about that team: a report that broke at the worst moment and fixes that came late. A better product couldn't outweigh that record.

cards.title: Trust: what customers buy when they can't check
body: In business buying, **trust** is the customer's belief that you will do what you said, and act in their interest in moments they can't see or control.
No contract covers every surprise. So business customers aren't only buying today's product. They're betting on how you'll behave next year, when something goes wrong.
Marketing researchers Robert Morgan and Shelby Hunt argued in 1994 that trust and commitment sit at the center of lasting business relationships.

image.label: A handshake bridge built from small kept promises
image.brief: 인포그래픽 스타일. 고객과 공급자 사이를 잇는 다리가 작은 벽돌로 만들어져 있고, 벽돌마다 "Called back", "On time", "Told us early" 같은 짧은 라벨. 다리 아래에 "Next year?"라고 적힌 안개 낀 미래 풍경.

cards.title: Trust is a track record, not a feeling.
body: Customers build it from evidence they collect over time:
list: **Small promises kept:** a callback when you said, a delivery on the agreed day
**Bad news told early:** before they find it themselves
**Knowing their business:** advice that fits their situation, not yours
**Low self-interest:** sometimes telling them not to buy
cards.callout: Consultants David Maister, Charles Green and Robert Galford put it as a rough formula: credibility, reliability and closeness, divided by how self-serving you seem.
cards.softwareNote: Trust shows up in outages and roadmaps. A company that posts honest incident updates and ships what it announced earns renewals. One that promises a feature to close a deal and never builds it can lose the account, even with a good product.

cards.title: Friendly is not the same as trusted.
body: Many people think a business relationship means lunches, gifts and remembering birthdays. Those create liking. Liking is pleasant, but it rarely survives a missed deadline.
Picture a supplier everyone enjoys who delivers late twice. Against a dull rival who always delivers on time, the dull rival usually keeps the account.
And trust is lopsided: it takes many kept promises to build and one hidden problem to lose.

cards.title: Trust can turn into inertia.
body: A trusted supplier often stays long after a better option appears. That protects you as the incumbent and makes life hard as the newcomer. But trust is not a substitute for value. If your price or quality slips, trust buys you time, not forever.
Trust also tends to sit with people, not companies. If one account manager holds every relationship, it can leave with them. Spread contact across your team.

cards.title: Now it's a building contractor.
body: You repair apartments for a property management company that sends you steady work. Halfway into a bathroom job, you find hidden water damage. The job will cost about 30% more than your quote.

image.label: Contractor photographing water damage behind a bathroom wall
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 욕실 벽 타일을 걷어낸 자리에 물에 젖은 얼룩이 보이고, 작업복 차림의 수리 기사가 휴대폰으로 사진을 찍는 장면. 실제 공구 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

options.text: Finish the job, then explain the extra cost on the invoice
options.feedback: The work gets done fast, but the manager learns about a big surprise when it's too late to decide. That's how steady clients start asking for second quotes.

options.text: Stop, send photos and a revised quote today, and let them choose
options.feedback: You lose a day and maybe some margin. You gain proof that your quotes and your word can be relied on, which is worth more than one job.

options.text: Absorb the extra cost quietly to keep them happy
options.feedback: Generous, and the client stays pleased. But they never learn what you did, and you've set a price you can't keep on the next job.

cards.title: Business customers buy your future behavior.
body: A better product opens the door. A record of kept promises keeps it open, especially when something goes wrong.
**Try it today:** list the promises you made to your three biggest customers this month. Mark any that slipped. Call about one before they call you.
